However, the evidence is thin. Every n-gram has a reported relative frequency of 0.000000, and no function-level locations or API/string context are given. All 20 n-grams are short, generic two-instruction mnemonic pairs that appear in nearly any compiled x86 code: control flow (TEST JZ, TEST JS, CMP JL, MOV JZ), calling conventions and stack handling (PUSH SUB, CALL ADD, ADD POP, LEA CALL), and data movement (XOR MOV, AND MOV, SUB MOV, MOV LEA). The conditional-move pairs (CMOVZ MOV, XOR CMOVNZ, CMP CMOVZ) and the bit-manipulation pairs (XOR XOR, XOR SHL) are the most suggestive, since they could reflect branchless, arithmetic-heavy code of the kind used in hashing loops. But they are not specific to mining. SHAP contributions are also small and evenly spread (+0.0063 to +0.0169), with no dominant signature. The model's score signals that the overall opcode profile resembles its malware training data, but this evidence alone cannot confirm mining behavior. The result is a strong model signal with weak, non-specific supporting evidence, so it is inconclusive and needs further analysis.
